\title{The Answer Key Picks the Winner: An Empirical Study of Import-Graph Reading Orders for Code Changes in Python}

\author{Neil Lunavat}
\affiliation{%
  \institution{\TODO{institution}}
  \country{\TODO{country}}}
\email{neillunavat3192@gmail.com}

\begin{abstract}
Before changing a file, a developer or an automated agent must decide what else to read, and
in what order. Many tools order files with the repository's dependency graph, but they are
evaluated against different notions of which files were ``needed''. We compare 30 ordering
methods (graph traversals, centrality rankings, clustering, lexical retrieval, change history,
and model-free adaptations of Aider, RepoGraph, LocAgent and CoSIL) on 3,123 tasks drawn from
1,873 real pull requests in 113 Python repositories (SWE-bench, SWE-bench-Live, SWE-rebench).
Each method starts from one changed file and returns an ordered list; we score how much of an
evidence-based answer key it covers per line read. Three findings stand out. (1) Graph methods
clearly beat random order: personalised PageRank on the undirected import graph reaches a mean
area under the coverage--cost curve of 0.436 versus 0.246 for random (A12 = 0.755); after
reading 4,000 lines it has found 48\% of the needed files versus 19\% for random order.
(2) The differences among the best graph methods are small (A12 $\leq$ 0.563), and a
seed-independent PageRank ranking already reaches 0.403. (3) The choice of answer key
reverses the ranking: on files co-edited in the pull request, BM25 is first and personalised
PageRank sixth; on files that define symbols the change uses, personalised PageRank is first
and BM25 fourteenth. Only 55\% of statically identified files were executed by the fixing
tests, and only 9\% of executed files were identified statically. We conclude that
evaluations of context retrieval for code changes should report results per evidence source,
and that graph proximity is a strong, cheap baseline that learned or agentic methods should be
required to beat. \TODO{execution-key results on the full sample; embedding baseline; RQ5 (does
order change the context an LLM needs?).}
\end{abstract}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}

A developer asked to change one file in an unfamiliar codebase must first decide what else to
read. The same question now faces automated agents that edit repositories: their context window
is finite, so the order in which files are read matters. A large family of tools answers the
question with the repository's dependency structure: they traverse or rank the import or call
graph around the file of interest~\cite{robillard2008topology,ouyang2025repograph,chen2025locagent,aiderrepomap}.
Others use lexical similarity~\cite{robertson2009bm25} or files that changed together in the
past~\cite{zimmermann2005mining,ying2004predicting}.

Comparing these approaches is harder than it looks, because ``the files that were needed'' is
not observable. Studies use proxies: the files edited by the same change, the files that define
names the change uses, or the files executed by tests that exercise the change. These proxies
are not interchangeable, and some are closer to the structure a given method uses than others.
If the answer key shares its construction with the method, the evaluation can reward the
method for agreeing with the key rather than for being useful.

We study this problem at the file level for Python, with the import graph as the structural
input. A \emph{method} receives one changed file (the \emph{seed}) and returns an ordered list
of other repository files. We score the list with a coverage--cost curve: the share of the
answer key read as a function of the number of lines read. We ask:

\begin{description}
\item[RQ1] How do ordering methods differ in how quickly they cover the answer key?
\item[RQ2] Do import-graph properties of a repository relate to which method performs best?
\item[RQ3] How far are the answer-key files from the seed in the import graph?
\item[RQ4] How does performance change when the seed is wrong?
\item[RQ5] Holding the file set fixed, does order change the context budget a language model
  needs? \TODO{not yet run; needs API budget.}
\end{description}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}
\item A pre-registered comparison of 30 model-free ordering methods and 5 references on 3,123
  tasks from 1,873 pull requests in 113 Python repositories, with a cost-aware metric and
  PR-level statistics (Section~\ref{sec:design}).
\item Evidence that the definition of the answer key changes which method wins, including a
  reversal between lexical and graph methods (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}).
\item A measurement of how far needed files lie from the changed file in the import graph, per
  evidence source (Section~\ref{sec:rq3}), and of how much the methods depend on a correct
  starting file (Section~\ref{sec:rq4}).
\item A replication package with the graph builder, the answer keys, all ordered lists and
  the analysis scripts. \TODO{archive DOI.}
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Background and Related Work}

\paragraph{Change impact analysis and program comprehension.}
Deciding what else a change touches is the classic change impact analysis
problem~\cite{bohner1996impact}. Studies of developers show that much maintenance time goes into
finding and relating relevant code~\cite{ko2006exploratory}. Robillard proposed ranking program
elements by the topology of their dependencies around a set of interest, using specificity and
reinforcement~\cite{robillard2008topology}; we adapt that algorithm to files. Feature location
surveys~\cite{dit2013feature} cover lexical, structural and dynamic techniques.

\paragraph{Change history.} Files that changed together in the past tend to change together
again~\cite{zimmermann2005mining,ying2004predicting}. We include a co-change ranking computed only
from commits strictly before each task's base commit.

\paragraph{Repository context for language-model agents.} Benchmarks built from real GitHub
issues and pull requests~\cite{jimenez2024swebench,badertdinov2025swerebench,zhang2025swebenchlive}
made file localization a measured step of automated repair. Tools build repository graphs for
this step: Aider's repository map ranks files by PageRank over a definition--reference
graph~\cite{aiderrepomap}; RepoGraph retrieves ego-graphs around relevant
definitions~\cite{ouyang2025repograph}; LocAgent lets an agent traverse a typed code
graph~\cite{chen2025locagent}; CoSIL searches a call graph~\cite{cosil2025}. Agentless localizes
hierarchically without an agent loop~\cite{xia2024agentless}. We re-implement the structural
core of four of these without a language model. These adaptations are not reproductions, and we
never compare our numbers to the published ones.

\section{Study Design}\label{sec:design}

All design choices, including the methods, metrics and statistics, were written down and
tagged in version control (\m{freeze-1}) before any method was run on any task. Deviations are
logged with reasons in the replication package.

\subsection{Repositories and pull requests}
We pooled task instances from SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench},
SWE-bench-Live~\cite{zhang2025swebenchlive} and SWE-rebench~\cite{badertdinov2025swerebench}.
A seeded random draw (seed 20260922) gave 1,886 pull requests from 113 repositories
(SWE-rebench 1,197; SWE-bench-Live 511; SWE-bench 178). Of these, 1,873 change at least one
existing non-test Python file that is a node of the import graph. The median repository has 158
Python source files (range 36--2,491), 506 import edges and 41,268 lines of Python (range
4,968--498,967). \TODO{selection criteria table: licence, size, line-cap rule, test exclusion.}

\subsection{Import graphs}
For each base commit we build a directed file-level graph with a custom parser based on
Python's \m{ast} module: an edge $a \rightarrow b$ means file $a$ imports a module defined by
file $b$. \m{from}-imports resolve to the module, imports of a package do not add edges to
parent \m{\_\_init\_\_.py} files, imports under \m{TYPE\_CHECKING} and inside functions are kept,
and edges are unweighted. Test files are excluded. \TODO{agreement check against a second
builder (tree-sitter) on the two pre-selected repositories.}

\subsection{Tasks and answer keys}
A pull request that edits $k$ existing source files that are graph nodes gives $k$ tasks: each
edited file in turn is the seed. This yields 3,123 tasks. For each task the answer key has three
sources, always kept separate and also combined:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Co-edited}: the other existing source files the pull request modifies.
\item \textbf{Symbol}: the files that define names used on the pull request's added lines,
  resolved with \m{jedi}.
\item \textbf{Execution}: files with a line inside a function body executed by a
  fail-to-pass test, recorded with \m{coverage.py} in the task's Docker image. Two variants (any
  executed line; excluding files also executed by an empty test) are kept for sensitivity.
\end{itemize}
The seed and files created by the pull request are never in a key. The \emph{union} key is the
union of the three sources; for tasks without an execution run it is the union of the two
static sources. Execution keys are currently available for 100 tasks (49 pull requests in 29
repositories). \TODO{execution keys for the remaining pull requests; the run was stopped by a
registry rate limit and is being resumed.}

\subsection{Methods}
Table~\ref{tab:methods} lists the families. Every method sees only the base commit: the import
graph, file sizes, identifiers, a definition--reference graph derived with \m{ast}, and git
history strictly before the base commit. No method sees the pull request, its tests or the
issue text, and none uses a language model. Ties and unordered sets are broken by a seeded
random permutation, and every method is run five times with different tie-break seeds.
\m{closure\_fwd\_trim} turned out to produce the same lists as \m{bfs\_fwd}; we keep both
for transparency. An embedding baseline was specified but not completed in time
\TODO{run on GPU and add}.

\subsection{Metric}
For a list $L$ and key $K$, coverage at budget $b$ is the share of $K$ contained in the longest
prefix of $L$ whose total length is at most $b$ lines. The primary score is the mean coverage
over the budgets $\{250, 500, \dots, 32000\}$ lines (eight doublings), which we call AUC; it lies
in $[0,1]$. Rank-based metrics (Acc@k, MRR, MAP, NDCG@10) are recorded for comparability.
\TODO{report file- and token-cost variants in an appendix.}

\subsection{Statistics}
The unit of analysis is the pull request: task scores are averaged within a pull request.
Methods are compared with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Vargha--Delaney
A12~\cite{vargha2000a12} as effect size, and Holm correction~\cite{holm1979}. Across repositories
we use the Friedman test with the Nemenyi post-hoc test~\cite{demsar2006}. For RQ2 we compute
Spearman correlations between each pre-listed graph property and each method's gain over random,
with Benjamini--Hochberg correction~\cite{benjamini1995}. Confidence intervals are 95\%
bootstrap intervals over repositories (2,000 resamples).

\section{Results}

\subsection{RQ1: How quickly do methods cover the answer key?}\label{sec:rq1}

\paragraph{Graph methods beat random order.}
Table~\ref{tab:rq1} shows the best methods on the union key (1,180 pull requests with a
non-empty key, 112 repositories). Personalised PageRank on the undirected graph
(\m{ppr\_und}) is first with AUC 0.436 (95\% CI 0.410--0.463), against 0.246 for random order
and 0.783 for the oracle ceiling. All methods in the table differ from random after Holm
correction. Figure~\ref{fig:curves} shows the curves: after 4,000 lines, \m{ppr\_und} has read
48\% of the key and random order 19\%; after 8,000 lines, 65\% and 34\%.

\paragraph{The top methods are close.}
The Friedman test rejects equal performance across repositories ($\chi^2 = 1893$, 112
repositories, 31 methods including random). \m{ppr\_und} has the best average rank (5.26) and
the Nemenyi critical difference is 4.57 ranks, so it is not separated from the next four methods
(\m{locagent\_bfs} 6.74, \m{ppr\_fwd} 7.14, \m{ids\_und} 7.36, \m{bfs\_und} 8.16). In pull-request-level
comparisons among the top eight methods, 18 of 28 pairs differ after Holm correction, but all
effects are small (A12 between 0.499 and 0.563). \m{ppr\_und} beats \m{locagent\_bfs} by 0.015
AUC (A12 0.516).

\paragraph{Much of the signal is global.}
Seed-independent PageRank, which gives the same list for every task in a repository, reaches
0.403: 92\% of the best method's AUC. Direction matters: following reverse imports
(\m{bfs\_rev} 0.154, \m{closure\_rev} 0.126) is worse than random, and so are Louvain
communities (0.226) and the seed's own directory (0.198).

\paragraph{The answer key reverses the ranking.}
Table~\ref{tab:bysource} splits the result by evidence source. On the \emph{symbol} key, which
is built from name definitions and therefore overlaps with import edges, graph methods lead
and \m{bm25} is 14th. On the \emph{co-edited} key, \m{bm25} is first (0.399), \m{cochange}
third, and \m{ppr\_und} sixth (0.356); forward BFS drops from 9th to 25th (0.229, below
random at 0.246). On the small execution key (49 pull requests), forward personalised
PageRank is first and \m{bm25} (0.250) is 16th. A study that used only one of these keys
would reach a different conclusion about which family is best.

\paragraph{Single-file versus multi-file changes.}
On pull requests that edit one source file (462), \m{ppr\_fwd} leads with 0.553 and
\m{bfs\_fwd} follows with 0.532. On multi-file pull requests (718), \m{ppr\_und} leads with
0.388, and \m{bm25} rises to 6th. In single-file changes, the key comes only from symbol
definitions (and execution where available), which again favours import-following methods.

\subsection{RQ2: Does repository structure predict the winner?}

Of 990 (property, method) pairs, 326 are significant after Benjamini--Hochberg correction. The
strongest associations are with size: the gain of \m{closure\_rev} over random correlates with
total lines ($\rho = 0.69$) and with the size of the largest import cycle ($\rho = 0.64$); the gain
of \m{bfs\_fwd} correlates with the number of import edges ($\rho = 0.63$). Size is linked to most
graph properties, so we treat these results as exploratory. The best method varies by
repository: 19 different methods win at least one repository, led by \m{ppr\_fwd} (20
repositories), \m{ppr\_und} (15) and \m{pagerank} (12). \TODO{partial correlations controlling
for size; minimum detectable $\rho$ for 112 repositories.}

\subsection{RQ3: How far are needed files from the seed?}\label{sec:rq3}

Table~\ref{tab:rq3} gives the shortest-path distance from the seed to each key file, ignoring
edge direction. Static key files are close: 88\% of co-edited and 87\% of symbol files lie within
two hops. Executed files are farther: 71.5\% within two hops, and most lie at exactly two hops. Very
few key files are unreachable (3--7\%). Direction matters: following imports only, 27--39\% of key
files cannot be reached at all, which explains why forward-only methods suffer on the co-edited
key.

\paragraph{The sources disagree.}
On the 100 tasks with an execution run, the static key has 3.2 files on average and the
execution key 20.0. Their mean Jaccard similarity is 0.18. Of the files in the static key, 55\%
were executed by the fail-to-pass tests; of the executed files, 9\% are in the static key.
\TODO{recompute on the full execution sample.}

\subsection{RQ4: What if the seed is wrong?}\label{sec:rq4}

We replaced the seed with a file one hop away, two hops away, or a random file, keeping the true
key (Table~\ref{tab:rq4}). All seed-dependent methods lose, but most stay above random when the
seed is only one or two hops off. With a random seed, BFS-style methods fall to about the random
floor (\m{bfs\_und} 0.246, \m{ids\_und} 0.247) and \m{bfs\_fwd} below it (0.198). Personalised
PageRank degrades gracefully (0.339 with a random seed) because it mixes in global
centrality. \m{cochange} collapses to almost zero (0.003), since the history of an unrelated
file says nothing about the change. Seed-independent \m{pagerank} and \m{indegree} are
unaffected, and with a wrong seed they are the best choice.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{For researchers.} The evidence source used as ground truth is not a detail. A key
built from symbol definitions rewards methods that follow imports; a key built from co-edited
files rewards lexical and historical similarity. Evaluations of localization and context
retrieval should report results per source, or state clearly which question their key answers.

\paragraph{For tool builders.} Personalised PageRank on the undirected import graph is a cheap,
model-free baseline that is at or near the top on every key. Seed-independent PageRank is
nearly as good and is the safer choice when the starting file is uncertain. Reverse-import
traversal, community detection and same-directory heuristics should not be used alone.

\paragraph{Headroom.} The oracle reaches 0.783 against 0.436 for the best method, so there is
room for better ordering. \TODO{RQ6: formal statement of the bounded-order problem and
its complexity; exact optima on small graphs.}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Threats to Validity}

\paragraph{Construct.} Every answer key is a proxy for ``needed'', and each is a lower bound on the
truly needed set. Symbol keys depend on \m{jedi} resolution; execution keys depend on the tests
the benchmark provides. Line count is one cost model; file and token costs are recorded.
\TODO{report the cost-model sensitivity.}

\paragraph{Internal.} Methods, metrics and statistics were fixed before any run. Bugs found
afterwards are listed in the replication package with their effect. Five tie-break runs reduce
the effect of random ordering. The execution key is so far available for only 49 pull
requests, so its results are preliminary. Co-change uses only commits before the base commit;
we checked for timestamp anomalies and found one rebase case that is a true ancestor.

\paragraph{External.} All repositories are Python projects drawn from three benchmarks of
issue-fixing pull requests, which favour well-tested libraries. The graph is file-level and
static; dynamic imports and plugin mechanisms are missed. Results may differ for other
languages and for finer-grained (function-level) graphs.

\paragraph{Conclusion.} We use the pull request as the unit, non-parametric paired tests,
effect sizes and multiple-comparison corrections. With about 1,180 pull requests, even
small differences are significant, so we base claims on effect sizes.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}

Starting from a changed file, a simple walk on the import graph (personalised PageRank) finds
the other needed files far faster than random reading: roughly half the needed files within
4,000 lines, against a fifth. But which method looks best depends on how ``needed'' is defined.
Graph methods win when the key comes from symbol definitions; lexical and history methods win
when it comes from co-edited files. The keys themselves overlap little. We recommend that
evaluations of code context retrieval report results per evidence source, and use graph
proximity as a baseline. \TODO{update after execution keys and RQ5.}
